title: Pip assessments are ‘not fit for purpose’, Timms tells MPs as he unveils his review – UK politics live
summary: Social security minister has been overseeing review designed to ‘rehumanise’ the system but Tories say it will lead to higher spending and fewer checks

blocks.text: Timms gives statement to MPs on his Pip review, setting out its three key conclusions
In the Commons, Stephen Timms is now delivering his statement on Pip.
He says Pip provides “vital support to deaf and disabled people and people with long term health conditions”. It was introduced 13 years ago, but has not been reviewed since then.

He says it was co-produced by himself, his two co-chair and 12 other members of a steering group. Almost all of those 12 people had “lived experience of disability or long term ill health”. Every member – including Timms himself – had just one vote, he says.
Timms says:

double quotation mark The review is clear that Pip remains a vital source of support, but it finds that the system is failing in three fundamental respects. First of all, the assessment is not fit for purpose. It doesn’t consider people’s needs, their aspirations, their barriers, or their extra costs. It’s just about what somebody cannot do. Many people find it adversarial and dehumanising. It struggles to reflect fluctuating and cumulative conditions properly, and it too often leaves people fearing that work, health, treatment or greater independence will count against them. Far from supporting independence, it can be a barrier to it. Second, awards do not consistently enable the right contribution toward the additional costs that people face. The areas of extra cost survey reviewed by the steering group showed that Pip does not always target the highest levels of support on those with the most severe needs. The future system should make the basis for support clearer, with decisions reflecting individual circumstances better. And third, the system’s offers offers too little scope for personalised solutions. The review recommends that cash should remain central, but that people should have the choice to access practical services as part of the overall support that they receive. That would allow the system to respond more flexibly to individual needs.

blocks.text: Steve Darling, the Lib Dem work and pensions secretary, praised Timms for working well with disabled people on the report. But it said it was interesting to note that Timms’ approach to young people was different from Alan Milburn’s. He urged the government to “get a grip on that”, and clarify its intentions.
IFS says proposals in Timms review for short-term changes to Pip would lead to 'likely increase' in spending

The Institute for Fiscal Studies thinktank has released its response to the Timms report. One point it makes is that the recommendations for short-term changes to Pip would probably lead to higher spending on the benefit.
Eduin Latimer, a senior research economist at the IFS, said:

double quotation markIn the short run, and while Pip continues in its current form, the Timms review recommends a range of changes to the application process, including making more of it available online, a fast-track process for those with severe disabilities, and providing an advocacy service to help applicants. Many of these proposals are intended to reduce the burden on applicants and make the process of applying easier. This has obvious benefits for applicants, but evidence from past reforms tells us it would likely increase the number of claimants – and hence spending.
In response to Whately, Timms said she was wrong to suggest that he was just proposing to tinker with the system. He was proposing a “fundamental new approach”, he said.
Tories claim Burnham has created welfare 'mess', with Timms and Milburn reports making recommendations 'poles apart'
Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, criticised the review for not proposing cuts to welfare spending in her response to Timms.
And she rejected his claim that his review overlapped with Milburn’s. She said:

double quotation markAlan Milburn also proposed changes to the disability benefit system, based on the plans we have set out shifting from cash to support for milder conditions and reducing the amount spent in total on sickness benefits. Two landmark reviews commissioned by the government landing one week apart, saying completely different things. The minister has tried to make out they fit together, that they have much in common, but pull the other one. They may have similar diagnoses, but their proposals are poles apart. What a mess. Which side is the prime minister going to pick? Team Milburn or Team Timms? Or will he freeze in the headlights and avoid the argument? Refuse to choose and create a two-tier system with one rule for under-25s and another for everyone else? This is no joke – £200bn, that’s what the working age welfare bill will cost taxpayers by the end of this parliament. But two and a half years after they’ve come into power, after two supposedly landmark reviews, they are no closer to doing anything about it to fix welfare, tackle soaring costs and get the benefits bill down.
Timms claims his report and Milburn's report have 'much in common' in their diagnoses
Timms said the government would consider the recommendations alongside the recommendations in the Milburn report.

double quotation markThe two reviews had different remits, but their diagnoses have much in common. Both find a fragmented system that asked people to prove what they cannot do, rather than understand what they could do with the right support. Both identify the worry that participation, treatment, or improvement could put somebody’s financial security at risk, and both argue for support that is more personalised, more joined up and more responsive to people’s lives. So, taken together, the two reviews share ambition for a system that offers security for those with the most severe needs.
Timms said the government did want to bring the benefits bill down, “but not through crude cuts that push people into hardship and increase costs elsewhere in the system”.
Timms says government accepting two of review's recommendations now, and others being considered
Timms says further work is needed on the way ahead.

double quotation markSupport should correspond more closely to genuine additional costs and needs. Cumulative and fluctuating impacts should be recognised properly, and the highest support should reflect the most severe needs. A good deal of further work is needed. The government will now undertake this work and set out its plans in next year’s white paper.
The report includes multiple recommendations. Timms says the government will consider them in full.
But the government can announce it is confirming two of them, he says.

double quotation markFirst, the people with serious well evidence conditions whose effects on daily life are clear should have access to a fast-track route without an unnecessary full assessment. That should include a distinct and rapid route for people at the end of life, as at present. But others should benefit from a fast-track as well. And second, that people whose health conditions are lifelong or degenerative, where there’s clear evidence that their functional needs are unlikely to improve, should not face repeated award reviews.
Timms says final decisions about future Pip eligibility rules will be matter for government and MPs
Timms says his review concluded “full system reform” was needed.

double quotation markThe review reaches the view that we need a full system reform, not just some adjustment of the forms or descriptors. It doesn’t prescribe a final set of eligibility rules because it recognises that decisions about eligibility criteria should sit with the elected government accountable to this house. But it does suggest principles on which those decisions should be made.
But the Green party has welcomed the Timms review. This is from the Green MP Siân Berry.

double quotation markThe long-awaited Timms review has clearly found the current situation to be dehumanising, harmful and counterproductive. And I agree the whole system should be made more responsive, specific and dependable to support equality and respect disabled people’s human rights. The rhetoric of insult and blame must end. It is so important for the government to recognise Pip is not an out of work benefit, to be chopped away and replaced by work support and that there should be no arbitrary age discrimination. I urge Stephen Timms to remind Alan Milburn of this.
Tories dismiss Timms review as 'complete farce', saying it will lead to more spending and fewer checks
Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, has described the Timms review as “a complete farce”. In a response, she said:

double quotation markThis review is a complete farce. After Labour abandoned welfare reform last year, all that is left is a review which will mean more spending, fewer checks, and a complete absence of substance. Labour’s flagship review into sickness benefits has failed. Labour will never cut welfare because they are the welfare party, and their leftwing backbenchers will never let them. The Conservatives will review the entire Pip system, remove eligibility for low-level mental health Pip claims, rapidly assess hundreds of thousands of additional claims and get Britain working again.
